title: Benchmarking Modular Optimization Strategies for Parameterized Quantum Circuits
authors: Carla Cotea, Stefan Balauca, Andreea Arusoaie
abstract: Training parameterized quantum circuits requires balancing optimization progress with limited evaluation budgets and the statistical uncertainty of near-term quantum hardware. We present a modular benchmarking framework that separates quantum search-direction estimation from classical parameter-update rules, allowing their interactions and sensitivities to be examined independently. We evaluate a suite of gradient-based, stochastic, and derivative-free optimizers across combinatorial optimization using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), supervised quantum machine learning using Iris classification and a quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) for binary MNIST classification, and quantum chemistry using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for molecular hydrogen. By separating objective evaluations from sample-circuit costs under finite-shot simulation and physical execution on a 156-qubit processor, we compare optimizer behavior across workloads with different parameter counts and measurement requirements. Four selected simulator and hardware case studies report terminal and best observed objectives separately, alongside post-training classifier accuracies. The comparisons include selected MaxCut and hydrogen trajectories and illustrate workload-dependent objective changes and evaluation costs, while the simulator benchmark compares both peak and mean performance across three seeds. The hardware runs do not establish an optimizer ranking or isolate a causal effect of device noise.

infographic.key_insight: A modular benchmarking framework cleanly separates quantum search-direction estimation from classical update rules to study how optimizers behave on parameterized quantum circuits under limited shots and evaluation budgets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps practitioners choose and test optimizer components for QAOA, QML, QCNN, and VQE workloads while accounting for parameter count, measurement cost, and hardware constraints.
method: Benchmarks gradient-based, stochastic, and derivative-free optimizers in a modular setup.
Tests on QAOA MaxCut, Iris classification, QCNN binary MNIST, and VQE for H2.
Compares simulator and 156-qubit hardware runs using finite-shot evaluations and separate cost accounting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports terminal and best objective values, post-training accuracies, and selected trajectories; simulator results are averaged over three seeds, while hardware runs use a real 156-qubit processor.
infographic.watch_item: The hardware experiments do not support an optimizer ranking or a causal claim about device noise.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Modular Optimization Strategies for Parameterized Quantum Circuits

title: Divide et Impera quantum neural networks for modular hybrid computing architectures
authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
abstract: Quantum machine learning is rapidly emerging as a promising and potentially more sustainable approach that can complement traditional, energy-hungry HPC, AI, and GPU resources-particularly for the demanding global challenges the world urgently needs to address. In recent years, the first prototypes of quantum processors have reached the market, are sometimes available via the cloud, and distributed quantum computing is beginning to move from a largely theoretical concept to a demonstrated reality. However, these devices are still noisy and qubit-limited. Therefore, it is desirable to design quantum machine learning models with a reduced quantum register and a limited number of quantum gates, avoiding overly deep and wide quantum circuits. Here, we explore this idea by proposing a novel divide-et-impera-based training protocol that splits quantum neural networks into smaller components and better governs their optimization. We benchmark our approach on real data and real-world prediction tasks in intertwined energy and environmental domains, such as the status of charging stations for electric vehicles and the global air quality index. Our results suggest a design principle for quantum machine learning algorithms across a wide range of applications, which can be more feasibly tested on state-of-the-art quantum processors or within modular quantum architectures being developed for future hybrid infrastructures interconnected via high-speed communication links.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a divide-et-impera training strategy that splits quantum neural networks into smaller modules to make quantum machine learning more trainable on noisy, qubit-limited hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This modular design could reduce circuit depth and register size, making quantum models more practical for near-term quantum processors and future distributed hybrid computing architectures.
method: Decompose a quantum neural network into smaller subcomponents
Train modules with a divide-and-conquer optimization protocol
Target low-depth, low-width circuits for noisy hardware
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is benchmarked on real data and real-world tasks, including electric-vehicle charging station status and global air quality index prediction.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on hardware noise, limited qubit counts, and the complexity of coordinating multiple quantum modules across distributed systems.
infographic.paper_title: Divide et Impera quantum neural networks for modular hybrid computing architectures

title: Quantum Optimization of the Color-of-Money Problem on IBM Quantum Hardware: A Proof-of-Concept Study
authors: Rahul Rana, Suman Kumar Roy, M Girish Chandra
abstract: The Color-of-Money (CoM) problem is a financial optimization challenge in which enterprises must determine how to allocate and route funds across multiple accounts, currencies, and time periods while satisfying regulatory, operational, and liquidity constraints. As the number of assets, obligations, and planning periods increases, the decision space grows rapidly, making large-scale optimization increasingly challenging for classical approaches. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept quantum implementation of the CoM problem using IBM Quantum hardware. The original optimization problem is formulated as a constrained Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem and transformed into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) representation suitable for quantum execution. We employ a Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) with Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE), a qubit efficient encoding technique and apply error-mitigation technique to improve solution fidelity on noisy quantum hardware. A prototype instance consisting of 3 assets, 3 obligations, and 2 time periods was executed on real IBM quantum hardware and benchmarked against classical exact solver SCIP. The quantum approach successfully reproduced the same optimal solution obtained classically, validating the correctness and feasibility of the proposed methodology. While current noisy quantum hardware does not outperform classical optimization on the evaluated small instance, the results demonstrate the feasibility of executing treasury optimization workloads on current quantum hardware and provide a foundation for future investigations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that a treasury optimization problem can be reformulated as a QUBO and solved on IBM quantum hardware with the same optimal answer as a classical exact solver on a small test instance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It demonstrates a practical pathway for mapping constrained financial scheduling and cash-flow allocation problems onto near-term quantum workflows.
method: Formulated the Color-of-Money problem as a constrained MILP.
Converted the MILP into a QUBO for quantum execution.
Used a VQA with Pauli Correlation Encoding and error mitigation on IBM hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: A prototype instance with 3 assets, 3 obligations, and 2 time periods was run on real IBM quantum hardware and matched the optimal solution from the SCIP exact solver.
infographic.watch_item: The validation is limited to a very small proof-of-concept instance, so scalability and performance on larger noisy problems remain unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Optimization of the Color-of-Money Problem on IBM Quantum Hardware: A Proof-of-Concept Study

title: Q-PhotoMarket: A Design Space Exploration Framework for Photonic Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks in Financial Market Prediction
authors: Alberto Marchisio, Hanzalah Mohamed Siraj, Muhammad Kashif, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Photonic quantum computing has recently emerged as a promising platform for hybrid quantum machine learning due to its native realization of linear-optical circuits and the computational complexity of boson sampling. However, despite growing interest in quantum methods for finance, the influence of photonic circuit design choices on predictive performance remains largely unexplored. Existing studies typically evaluate a single architecture, leaving the broader photonic design space unexamined. In this work, we present Q-PhotoMarket, a systematic design space exploration (DSE) framework for photonic hybrid quantum neural networks (HQNNs) applied to financial market prediction. We explore over 5,000 valid photonic configurations spanning input photon states, circuit architectures, entangling models, and measurement strategies across their compatible computation spaces, for U.S., Indian, and cryptocurrency markets. To improve search efficiency, the exhaustive exploration is complemented with Bayesian optimization. We further incorporate threshold calibration and prediction-collapse diagnostics to enable reliable evaluation under increasingly imbalanced return thresholds. Experimental results show that systematic exploration of more than 5,000 photonic HQNN configurations reveals consistent architectural patterns across financial markets, identifies robust high-performing designs, and demonstrates competitive performance relative to classical machine learning baselines.

infographic.key_insight: Q-PhotoMarket shows that photonic hybrid quantum neural network performance for market prediction depends strongly on circuit design choices, and that systematic exploration can uncover robust architectures rather than relying on a single hand-picked model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a practical design-space exploration workflow for photonic quantum ML, helping engineers compare viable circuit configurations and benchmark them against classical baselines for finance tasks.
method: Explored 5,000+ valid photonic HQNN configurations across input states, circuit architectures, entangling models, and measurement strategies.
Applied Bayesian optimization to accelerate the search over the compatible photonic design space.
Added threshold calibration and prediction-collapse diagnostics for more reliable evaluation on imbalanced return-threshold settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports experiments across U.S., Indian, and cryptocurrency markets, finding consistent architectural patterns and competitive performance versus classical machine learning baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Because the search space is large and evaluation depends on threshold calibration, results may be sensitive to dataset imbalance, market regime, and the specific photonic constraints used to define valid configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Q-PhotoMarket: A Design Space Exploration Framework for Photonic Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks in Financial Market Prediction

title: Measurement-Efficient Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search for Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Lukas Theißinger, Thore Gerlach, Christian Bauckhage
abstract: Differentiable quantum architecture search (DQAS) is a promising framework for the automated design of quantum circuits, particularly for variational quantum optimization algorithms. However, its practical deployment on quantum hardware is limited by the large number of circuit measurements required during optimization, making hardware execution costly. In this work, we show that for a broad class of combinatorial optimization problems and commonly used rotational gate parameterizations, the measurement cost of DQAS can be significantly reduced without changing the optimization objective. We derive the proposed measurement reduction scheme theoretically and validate it experimentally on 3-SAT and MaxCut benchmark problems. Our approach reduces the requested gradient measurement cost by about 39 to 41% while introducing only negligible classical post-processing overhead, lowering the practical cost of executing DQAS on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that differentiable quantum architecture search for combinatorial optimization can cut circuit-measurement cost substantially without changing the optimization objective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes DQAS more practical on near-term quantum hardware by reducing one of the main bottlenecks: expensive gradient estimation during circuit search and training.
method: Derive a measurement-reduction scheme for a broad class of combinatorial optimization problems.
Exploit commonly used rotational gate parameterizations to reuse or avoid redundant gradient measurements.
Add only negligible classical post-processing while preserving the original optimization objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors validate the method experimentally on 3-SAT and MaxCut benchmarks, reporting about 39–41% lower requested gradient measurement cost.
infographic.watch_item: The gain depends on the assumed problem class and gate parameterization, so applicability may be narrower outside the studied DQAS setting.
infographic.paper_title: Measurement-Efficient Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search for Combinatorial Optimization

title: On the Expressive Power and Capacity of Quantum Data Reuploaders
authors: Lord Sen, Shyamapada Mukherjee
abstract: Data reuploading---repeatedly encoding classical inputs at multiple layers of a parameterized quantum circuit---is a central mechanism for enhancing the expressivity of quantum neural networks (QNNs). Building on the Fourier-theoretic framework of Schuld et al.~\cite{schuld2021fourier}, we study the frequency spectrum of the general multivariate, $R$-reupload architecture (QDR). (i) We make explicit that the accessible frequencies form the set $K_R=S^{(R)}-S^{(R)}$, which equals the $R$-fold sumset $T^{(R)}$ of the difference set $T=S-S$ of the encoding spectrum, and we characterise it exactly: $K_R=\{k\in\mathcal L:\ \ell_T(k)\le R\}$, where $\mathcal L=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb Z}(T)$ is an integer lattice and $\ell_T$ is word length in $T$. (ii) We show that the \emph{directions} of the spectrum stabilise already at $R=1$ (the real span of $K_R$ equals that of $\mathcal L$), whereas the spectrum itself never saturates: the maximal frequency grows linearly in $R$ and the number of frequencies grows polynomially, as $Θ(R^{m})$ with $m=\mathrm{rank}\,\mathcal L$. (iii) Using the spectrum size, we give a Rademacher-complexity bound on the capacity of QDRs of order $\sqrt{|K_R|/n}$. (iv) We report experiments on function approximation and classification with train/test splits, several seeds and parameter-matched classical baselines. The simulated spectra match the theory exactly. A single-qubit QDR beats a matched MLP on several smooth or periodic univariate targets and on the spiral task, but it is clearly worse on multivariate regression ($d\ge4$), where it is highly sensitive to the input-encoding scale; it beats the MLP only on equations with $d\le3$ inputs.

infographic.key_insight: Data reuploading expands a quantum model’s usable frequency spectrum in a precisely characterizable way, but its expressive growth is polynomial and capacity scales with the number of accessible frequencies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a practical rule for designing quantum neural networks: reuploading increases expressivity, yet performance depends strongly on encoding choice, input dimension, and the resulting capacity-cost tradeoff.
method: Derive the accessible Fourier frequencies of an R-reupload quantum circuit as a repeated sumset of the encoding spectrum.
Characterize the spectrum exactly via integer-lattice word length and show its directions stabilize after one reupload while its size grows polynomially.
Use the spectrum size to obtain a Rademacher-complexity capacity bound for quantum data reuploaders.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on function approximation and classification, with train/test splits and matched baselines, show the simulated spectra agree with theory and that a single-qubit QDR can outperform an MLP on some low-dimensional or periodic tasks but not on harder multivariate regression.
infographic.watch_item: The model is highly sensitive to input-encoding scale and becomes weak relative to classical baselines on higher-dimensional regression, so careful encoding calibration is essential.
infographic.paper_title: On the Expressive Power and Capacity of Quantum Data Reuploaders

title: Quantum anomaly detection in real scarce data
authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
abstract: Anomaly detection on small and unbalanced datasets remains very challenging in machine learning, although this scenario is common in several domains, including healthcare, cybersecurity, finance, and energy. Data augmentation and generative AI may mitigate training-data scarcity, but they often fall short because anomalies are, by definition, unpredictable, rare, and highly diverse events compared to high-probability normal data. Overfitting to pseudo-anomalies, model collapse, high-dimensional data, uninterpretable black-box models, and validation challenges are typical issues limiting their practical applicability. In this context, quantum machine learning may provide a promising and more sustainable avenue because it can enable more interpretable models with far fewer trainable parameters and smaller datasets, implementable on energy-efficient quantum hardware. Here, we propose a novel two-step hybrid classical--quantum architecture for sequential data and test it on a realistic scenario in the global energy-transition domain, i.e., automated anomaly detection in large-scale photovoltaic plants. The achieved generalization capability and competitive prediction accuracy may pave the way for new hybrid learning models able to exploit the continuously increasing power of cloud-available and more sustainable quantum accelerators integrated with more traditional energy-hungry High Performance Computing resources.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid classical–quantum model can improve anomaly detection on scarce, highly imbalanced sequential data by using fewer trainable parameters and a more interpretable architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach is relevant for real-world monitoring systems like large-scale photovoltaic plants, where rare faults must be detected reliably under limited labeled data and tight energy-efficiency constraints.
method: Two-step hybrid classical–quantum architecture for sequential anomaly detection
Designed for small, unbalanced datasets where anomalies are rare and diverse
Evaluated on a realistic photovoltaic-plant anomaly detection scenario
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive prediction accuracy and strong generalization on a realistic large-scale photovoltaic plant use case.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment still depends on robust validation under scarce-label conditions and on access to stable, scalable quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum anomaly detection in real scarce data

title: Connectivity Controls Variational Accessibility in Symmetry-Preserving Quantum Circuits
authors: Sahinur Reja
abstract: Designing expressive quantum circuits for the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a central challenge in simulating interacting many-body systems. Even symmetry-preserving (SP) circuits need not access the full many-body symmetry sector. We demonstrate this explicitly for the spin-$1/2$ XXZ and Hubbard models, where Hamiltonian-inspired nearest-neighbor (NN) SP circuits generate restricted dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs). While these restricted manifolds can accurately represent the ground state near the free-fermion limits, $J_z=0$ for XXZ and $U=0$ for Hubbard, interactions expose inaccessible many-body directions and severely limit VQE performance even at large circuit depth. Remarkably, a minimal modification of the generator connectivity can reconstruct the full orthogonal DLA within all relevant symmetry sectors studied in this work. For XXZ model, the addition of {\it only} one SP next-to-NN single-excitation connection triggers this dramatic reconstruction, whereas the Hubbard case requires a SP correlated double-excitation;--showing that the relevant connectivity can extend from the spatial lattice to many-body configuration space. This reconstruction enlarges the tangent space and accessibility of the energy-lowering Hamiltonian direction, leading to near-unit ground-state fidelity in VQE simulations. Our results establish a direct link between generator connectivity and variational accessibility and suggest a broader circuit-design principle: identify minimal symmetry-preserving generators that enlarge the accessible many-body space rather than increasing circuit depth alone. This perspective may have broader relevance for quantum many-body simulation at the interface of condensed-matter physics and quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: In symmetry-preserving VQE circuits, generator connectivity—not circuit depth alone—determines whether the ansatz can access the full many-body symmetry sector and reach high-fidelity ground states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A minimal, well-chosen symmetry-preserving connectivity upgrade can dramatically improve quantum simulation performance, reducing the need to stack deeper circuits that still remain variationally restricted.
method: Studied symmetry-preserving nearest-neighbor circuits for the XXZ and Hubbard models via dynamical Lie algebra analysis.
Added one minimal extra generator: a next-to-nearest-neighbor single-excitation for XXZ or a correlated double-excitation for Hubbard.
Compared how these connectivity changes expand the accessible manifold and improve VQE ground-state optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the restricted circuits work near free-fermion limits, but interactions expose inaccessible directions; the minimal connectivity change reconstructs the full orthogonal DLA and yields near-unit ground-state fidelity in VQE simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The required generator modification is model-specific, so identifying the right symmetry-preserving connectivity may still be nontrivial for new Hamiltonians or hardware-constrained layouts.
infographic.paper_title: Connectivity Controls Variational Accessibility in Symmetry-Preserving Quantum Circuits

title: Pauli Flat Quantum States Mimicking Maximal Magic
authors: Paweł Cieśliński
abstract: Quantum magic is a necessary resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, capturing the departure of quantum states from the classically simulable stabiliser set. Motivated by its role in quantum information processing, we investigate the correlation structure of states that maximize the Rényi stabiliser entropies, focusing on the T-type and Hoggar states. Inspired by their distinctive properties, we explore the notion of Pauli flat states, defined as N-qubit states whose expectation values on all Pauli strings are equal in absolute value. These states reproduce the correlation structure of highly magical states, which could also be interpreted as a mixed variant of Pauli covariant N-qubit symmetric informationally complete (SIC) Weyl-Heisenberg fiducial states, while not necessarily possessing nontrivial quantum magic. We investigate their existence and possible constructions, including examples both inside and outside of the stabiliser polytope. To identify the latter, we examine a magic witness tailored to the introduced family of states. Finally, we discuss their entanglement and Bell nonlocality, providing a broader characterization of their quantum properties. For completeness, we find pure states with a relaxed condition on the Pauli expectations, which forces unequal elements to zero, and discuss their non-stabiliserness. Our results offer a new perspective on the relation between quantum magic and Pauli correlation structures. They hold relevance to geometrical approaches to quantum mechanics, entanglement and magic detection, as well as estimation tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Pauli-flat states have uniform Pauli-string magnitudes and can mimic the correlation patterns of highly magical quantum states, even when they are not genuinely magical.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum engineers a new state family and witness tools for probing magic, entanglement, and Bell nonlocality in fault-tolerant quantum workflows.
method: Define N-qubit Pauli-flat states by equal absolute expectation values over all Pauli strings.
Compare their correlation structure to T-type and Hoggar states and to Pauli-covariant SIC fiducials.
Use a tailored magic witness to separate states inside vs. outside the stabilizer polytope.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports explicit existence/construction examples, including states both inside and outside the stabilizer polytope, plus pure-state variants under a relaxed Pauli-expectation condition.
infographic.watch_item: Uniform Pauli correlations can resemble maximal magic without guaranteeing nontrivial magic, so correlation-based screening alone may misclassify states.
infographic.paper_title: Pauli Flat Quantum States Mimicking Maximal Magic

title: Protecting bosonic codes from ancilla-induced errors with continuous-variable flags
authors: Thomas Décultot, Ronan Gautier, Mazyar Mirrahimi
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction represents a route towards significant hardware overhead reduction for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, controlling quantum harmonic oscillators that encode the quantum information comes with its own challenges. In many platforms such as superconducting circuits and trapped ions, the bosonic degree of freedom is controlled by an ancillary qubit whose decay during a qubit-oscillator gate propagates to the oscillator as a continuous error. Such errors generally lie beyond the scope of errors that the bosonic code is capable of correcting. We introduce the continuous-variable flag: an auxiliary oscillator coupled to the ancilla whose phase-space position encodes the continuous error corrupting the storage mode. After the gate, a heterodyne measurement of the flag estimates this continuous-variable error and a subsequent feedback control undoes it up to a bosonic code stabilizer. The scheme requires no new ingredients, as the flag is driven by the same dispersive coupling, displacements and rotations that implement the gates it is supposed to protect. We construct sequences protecting conditional rotations to all orders in ancilla decay with one flag, and conditional displacements to first order with one flag and to all orders with two. Simulations with realistic circuit-QED parameters predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer logical errors for the parity measurement of a four-component cat code, and a finite-energy GKP logical lifetime near its noiseless-ancilla bound. By discretizing continuous-variable errors, the flags introduced in this work are a useful tool for any hybrid oscillator-qubit processor, and open the route towards fault-tolerant simulation and computation with bosonic modes.

infographic.key_insight: A continuous-variable flag oscillator can record ancilla decay as a measurable phase-space shift, allowing feedback to undo continuous errors on bosonic codes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives hybrid qubit-oscillator platforms a practical way to suppress ancilla-induced gate errors using only standard dispersive couplings, displacements, rotations, and heterodyne readout.
method: Couple a flag oscillator to the ancilla so decay-induced errors are mapped into the flag's phase-space position.
Heterodyne-measure the flag after the gate to estimate the continuous error.
Apply feedback to correct the storage mode, up to a bosonic code stabilizer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations with realistic circuit-QED parameters report more than three orders of magnitude fewer logical errors for a four-component cat-code parity measurement and a GKP logical lifetime near the noiseless-ancilla limit.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on accurate flag readout and feedback, and the correction is designed around specific gate sequences and error models.
infographic.paper_title: Protecting bosonic codes from ancilla-induced errors with continuous-variable flags

title: Binary Optimization of Measurement Groupings for Quantum Energy Estimation
authors: Isaac L. Huidobro-Meezs, Rodrigo A. Vargas-Hernández
abstract: Repeated measurements can dominate the resources required for quantum energy estimation, making the choice of which Pauli observables to measure together a central optimization problem for variational quantum algorithms. We formulate fully commuting measurement grouping as a classical binary optimization problem based on clique selection and construct non-overlapping groups using mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). For a benchmark of molecular Hamiltonians, groupings optimized with approximate covariances reduce the non-overlapping measurement requirement $\varepsilon^2M$ by $51.8\%$ on average relative to sorted insertion (SI). Using the MILP groups to initialize iterative coefficient splitting (ICS), denoted MILP-ICS, yields an average $24.3\%$ reduction relative to ICS initialized from SI (SI-ICS). The optimized groups also transfer across nearby molecular geometries while preserving substantial measurement savings. We further introduce O-clique, which directly optimizes overlapping commuting supports through candidate-clique selection and coefficient profiles. Although O-clique provides only modest additional reductions beyond MILP-ICS, it reduces the measurement requirement by $27.3\%$ on average relative to SI-ICS with 100 iterations, despite using only five final coefficient refinement iterations, indicating improved support quality. Finally, we extend the comparison to Fermi--Hubbard, Kitaev--Heisenberg--$Γ$, and XYZ lattice Hamiltonians, where MILP-based groupings substantially outperform the corresponding SI-based strategies. Together, these results show that variance-informed optimization of measurement-group structure can substantially reduce sampling costs across molecular and lattice Hamiltonians, with optimized non-overlapping groups providing strong, transferable initializations and direct overlapping optimization offering further gains.

infographic.key_insight: Choosing how to group commuting Pauli measurements can be cast as a binary optimization problem, and optimizing these groups materially reduces the sampling cost of quantum energy estimation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work provides a practical route to lower measurement overhead in variational quantum algorithms, which can directly improve efficiency on near-term quantum hardware.
method: Formulate fully commuting measurement grouping as a MILP clique-selection problem for non-overlapping groups.
Use optimized groups as initialization for iterative coefficient splitting (MILP-ICS) to improve overlapping measurement strategies.
Introduce O-clique to optimize overlapping commuting supports via candidate-clique selection and coefficient profiles.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across benchmark molecular Hamiltonians, approximate-covariance optimized groupings reduced the non-overlapping measurement requirement by 51.8% on average versus sorted insertion, and MILP-based methods also outperformed SI-based strategies on lattice Hamiltonians.
infographic.watch_item: The best performance depends on covariance approximations and optimization overhead, so the method may be less attractive if classical preprocessing cost is too high for the target problem size.
infographic.paper_title: Binary Optimization of Measurement Groupings for Quantum Energy Estimation

title: Quantum Approximation Complexity of Classical Optimization Problems
authors: Stuart Hadfield
abstract: Classical approximation complexity asks what solution quality can be guaranteed with polynomial-time computation. The classes APX, PTAS, and FPTAS distinguish a fixed approximation ratio, approximation to any fixed accuracy, and approximation schemes whose running time is also polynomial in inverse accuracy. Their randomized counterparts are R-APX, R-PTAS, and R-FPTAS. We define bounded-error quantum counterparts BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, and BQ-FPTAS. Membership requires a uniform quantum algorithm that, on every input, returns a feasible classical solution achieving at least the claimed approximation ratio with probability at least 2/3. Scores (objective values) must be efficiently classically computable. Running time includes parameter selection, preparation, measurement, decoding, and repetition. Many quantum optimization methods are used heuristically, and high benchmark scores alone do not establish these guarantees. We further establish a conditional hierarchy for logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential approximation factors. Assuming NP $\subsetneq$ BQP, the quantum classes form a strict hierarchy. Problems based on prime factorization and discrete logarithms give conditional quantum-classical separations. Certified Maximum Order has an exact quantum algorithm, while any randomized polynomial-time algorithm guaranteeing at least an inverse-polynomial approximation ratio on every input would yield efficient factoring. Discrete-Logarithm Fitting has an exact quantum algorithm and a deterministic one-half approximation, but any fixed improvement over one half would give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the safe-prime discrete logarithm problem. Our results show, under explicit complexity assumptions, that quantum computation can improve worst-case approximation guarantees. A quantum-classical gap for common problems such as MaxCut or MaxSAT remains open.

infographic.key_insight: The paper defines bounded-error quantum approximation classes and shows that, under standard complexity assumptions, quantum algorithms can certify better worst-case approximation guarantees than classical randomized algorithms for some optimization problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a formal benchmark for judging whether a quantum optimization method is truly better than a heuristic by requiring provable approximation ratios and polynomial-time guarantees.
method: Define BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, and BQ-FPTAS as quantum analogues of classical approximation classes.
Require a uniform quantum algorithm that outputs a feasible classical solution with at least 2/3 success probability and efficiently computable objective scores.
Use complexity-theoretic reductions to prove conditional separations and hierarchy results for specific number-theoretic optimization problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports conditional proofs and example problems—Certified Maximum Order and Discrete-Logarithm Fitting—rather than experimental benchmarks or numerical datasets.
infographic.watch_item: These are worst-case complexity guarantees under explicit assumptions, so benchmark performance or heuristic success alone does not establish membership in the new quantum approximation classes.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Approximation Complexity of Classical Optimization Problems

title: Efficient Estimation of Logical Sensitivities Through Fault-Counting
authors: Winston Fu, J. Wilson Staples, Jeff D. Thompson
abstract: Quantum error-correcting circuits are affected by multiple physical noise mechanisms, whose contributions to logical failure must be understood to evaluate code performance and guide improvements in hardware. The individual error budget contributions for an error type $i$ can be characterized by its logical sensitivity $ν_i = \frac{\partial p_L}{\partial p_i}$, which measures the response of the logical error rate $p_L$ to each physical noise parameter $p_i$. Normally, $ν_i$ is measured using linear fits such as finite differences, where $p_L$ is measured at two or more values of $p_i$ to calculate partial derivatives. In this paper, we develop a differentiable estimator to obtain all components of $\nabla_{\mathbf p}p_L$ simultaneously from a single Monte Carlo data set at one noise configuration, using information about the underlying fault configurations. In surface code simulations with circuit-level noise, the estimator agrees with conventional finite differences while requiring one to two orders of magnitude fewer shots to achieve the same variance. We apply this technique to quantify error budgets, resolve sensitivities at the individual qubit level, and infer effective code distance. Finally, we incorporate the sensitivities into Newton root finding to locate and trace threshold contours in multidimensional noise models. These results provide an efficient method for extracting and applying logical sensitivity information from standard quantum error correction simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A single fault-counting Monte Carlo run can estimate all logical sensitivities of a quantum error-correcting code at once, replacing many separate finite-difference sweeps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives hardware and QEC engineers a much cheaper way to identify dominant noise sources, localize weak qubits, and map threshold behavior in multidimensional noise models.
method: Differentiate logical error rate with respect to each physical noise parameter using fault-count information from one simulation data set.
Estimate the full gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf p} p_L\) simultaneously instead of one parameter at a time.
Use the sensitivities for error-budget analysis, qubit-level diagnostics, effective code-distance inference, and Newton-based threshold tracing.
infographic.evidence_signal: In surface-code simulations with circuit-level noise, the estimator matched finite differences while using roughly 10x to 100x fewer shots for the same variance.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on access to underlying fault configurations, so implementation must be compatible with the simulator or sampling pipeline.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Estimation of Logical Sensitivities Through Fault-Counting

title: Demonstration of Parallel Multi-QPU Execution for Fragment-Based Quantum Chemistry Using On-Premises Hardware
authors: Nils Herrmann, Mariam Akhtar, Luke W. Bertels, Leigh Cameron, Raymond Chan, Lei Cheng
abstract: Fragment molecular orbital (FMO) quantum chemistry offers a natural route to parallel quantum computing: large molecular calculations can be decomposed into smaller quantum subproblems that can, in principle, run concurrently. Their practical benefit on real quantum hardware, however, has remained unclear. We demonstrate parallel FMO calculations on three room-temperature diamond-based 'Quoll' quantum computers installed on-site at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Helium clusters (He$_{n}$, $n=2,4,8,10,14$) served as a testbed for total energy calculations using the Quantum Wave Function Sampler (QWFS), a selected configuration interaction (SCI) approach. We compare two execution modes: synchronous shot-parallel execution, in which quantum processors jointly sample QWFS circuits and combine their SPAM-corrected counts into a single probability distribution; and asynchronous fragment-parallel execution, in which processors independently evaluate FMO fragments using device-specific optimized circuits. Both modes increase quantum sampling throughput without systematic loss of accuracy. The three-QPU shot-parallel workflow reaches a parallel efficiency of $93.60\%$, while the fragment-parallel workflow achieves a measured efficiency of $75.01\%$, increasing to $95.17\%$ when excluding the non-useful idle time associated with non-interruptible submitted jobs. In both cases, the assembled FMO-QWFS energies remain chemically accurate compared to the classical ideal. These results provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that parallel quantum execution can improve the practical throughput of quantum chemistry workflows on prototype hardware, motivating the development of future HPC environments with many fault-tolerant quantum processors operating as a distributed resource for molecular and materials simulation.

infographic.key_insight: Parallel execution across multiple on-premises QPUs can speed up fragment-based quantum chemistry without sacrificing chemical accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work shows how future HPC systems could treat several quantum processors as a distributed resource to increase throughput for molecular simulation workflows.
method: Use fragment molecular orbital (FMO) decomposition to split a molecule into smaller quantum chemistry subproblems.
Compare synchronous shot-parallel execution with asynchronous fragment-parallel execution on three room-temperature diamond-based QPUs.
Run Quantum Wave Function Sampler (QWFS) selected configuration interaction calculations on helium clusters and assemble SPAM-corrected results.
infographic.evidence_signal: On helium clusters He$_n$ (n=2, 4, 8, 10, 14), the three-QPU workflow achieved 93.60% parallel efficiency for shot-parallel execution and 75.01% for fragment-parallel execution, rising to 95.17% after excluding idle time, while maintaining chemically accurate energies.
infographic.watch_item: The reported efficiency depends on non-interruptible job scheduling and device-specific circuit optimization, so real-world gains may drop if orchestration or hardware availability is less favorable.
infographic.paper_title: Demonstration of Parallel Multi-QPU Execution for Fragment-Based Quantum Chemistry Using On-Premises Hardware

title: When Expressivity Is Not Enough: Discrete Routing Geometry in Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Yu Wang
abstract: Finding useful variational quantum circuits requires more than representational capacity: training must also have access to directions that improve the objective. We study how discrete CNOT routing shapes both capacity and local accessibility. For circuits built from CNOT and arbitrary one-qubit gates, we separate binary routing matrices from continuous rotations to relate global capacity to local tangent accessibility. An exact finite-field formula for the operator Schmidt rank of a CNOT block and cumulative multiblock bounds yield capacity constraints and a Bell-pair fidelity obstruction. Locally, routing propagates generators into a routing-dependent tangent space, so all parameter gradients can vanish even when the ambient objective gradient is nonzero; frame bounds distinguish loss of gradient coverage from poor conditioning. A routing-conditioned identity insertion preserves the current unitary, state, loss, and existing gradients while adding new tangent directions. Candidate-only and incremental projection scores provide local criteria for ranking insertions. Exact-statevector tests show strong short-horizon score-descent correlations on controlled Bell tasks and effective equal-cost selection on connected Heisenberg chains up to twelve qubits, with complementary TFIM selector controls. A broader TFIM routing ensemble exhibits routing-dependent near-stagnation. Together, these results connect representational capacity, local accessibility, and same-point repair through a common discrete routing description. An architecture need not remain fixed during training: task-dependent geometric information can guide the opening of new descent directions while preserving the learned circuit at insertion. This provides a concrete local approach to a broader problem: how useful quantum circuits can be discovered from the information a task supplies.

infographic.key_insight: Discrete CNOT routing can limit not only the expressive capacity of a variational quantum circuit, but also whether training can actually access useful descent directions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum circuit design and optimization, routing choices should be treated as a trainability problem, not just a hardware-compatibility or expressivity problem.
method: Separate binary routing matrices from continuous one-qubit rotations.
Derive exact capacity and local tangent-space bounds for CNOT-routed circuits.
Use routing-conditioned identity insertion to add new descent directions without changing the current unitary.
infographic.evidence_signal: Exact-statevector experiments on Bell tasks and Heisenberg/TFIM benchmarks show strong short-horizon score-descent correlations and routing-dependent near-stagnation effects.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed scores and routing updates are evaluated in controlled settings, so their robustness on noisy hardware and larger-scale ansatzes still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: When Expressivity Is Not Enough: Discrete Routing Geometry in Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Designing Group-Valued Codes with Full Regular Low-Weight Bases
authors: Jong Yeon Lee
abstract: Efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures benefit from low-weight logical operators. However, reported canonical bases for high-rate, high-distance codes can be several times heavier than the code distance, and fundamental obstructions can prevent minimum-weight logical operators from forming a complete canonical basis. To address this issue, we develop design principles for group-valued quantum error-correcting codes with low-weight full regular canonical logical bases, generated by translating a set of seed operators. We introduce frame width $f$, the smallest weight cutoff that permits a complete canonical logical basis, as an additional code parameter alongside distance $d$ and check weight $w$. Cataloguing these parameters together with explicit logical bases can inform resource estimates and the compilation of fault-tolerant logical operations. First, we identify a structural obstruction: for fully populated binary monomial CSS checks over a group of odd order, full regularity forces distance two, while for groups of power-of-two order, full row rank of both check matrices after replacing every group element by $1$ guarantees full regularity. Second, we demonstrate our principles through explicit high-rate lifted-product (LP) and pair-partition (PP) codes: an $[[1088,128,22]]$ LP code with $f=22$ and an $[[1024,256,24]]$ PP code with $f \leq 27$, both at $w=10$. At $w=11$, our PP constructions attain either $d=25$ with $f \leq 27$ or $d=24$ with the proved optimum $f=25$, demonstrating both a tradeoff among these parameters and a strict separation between distance and frame width. Finally, we propose a method combining symmetry reduction and stabilizer-based pruning for exhaustive distance certification, and use it to efficiently establish exact distances for LP examples with more than a thousand qubits.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces frame width as a new design parameter for quantum codes, showing that low-weight logical bases can exist only when code structure and symmetry constraints are carefully matched.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For fault-tolerant quantum computing, these results help estimate qubit and compilation overheads more accurately by pairing code distance with the actual weight of a complete logical basis.
method: Define frame width f as the smallest weight cutoff that still allows a full canonical logical basis.
Analyze structural obstructions and sufficient conditions for group-valued CSS codes, including odd-order vs. power-of-two group behavior.
Demonstrate the framework on high-rate lifted-product and pair-partition codes, plus a symmetry-reduction distance-certification workflow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports explicit examples including an [[1088,128,22]] lifted-product code with f=22 and an [[1024,256,24]] pair-partition code with f≤27, alongside exact distance certification for codes with more than a thousand qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Frame width is not always equal to distance, so designers should not assume minimum-weight logical operators form a complete canonical basis.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Group-Valued Codes with Full Regular Low-Weight Bases

title: Optimized discrete Wigner representations and non-stabilizerness in qubit systems
authors: A. B. Klimov, C. Muñoz, I. Sainz
abstract: The apparent absence of a stabilizer-speci?c phase-space description for qubit systems is not fundamental, but arises from ?xing a state-independent discrete Wigner map. Allowing the phase-space representation to adapt to the state through a simple optimization procedure, we prove that every qubit stabilizer state admits an exact delta-function discrete Wigner representation for any ?xed phase-space partition. This optimization can be implemented directly at the level of measurement statistics by selecting maximal probabilities across mutually unbiased bases forming the partition. This construction naturally leads to a non-stabilizer witness de?ned by the optimized value of the Wigner function at the origin. Stabilizer states saturate the universal lower bound of this witness for pure states, whereas a value strictly larger than the bound certi?es non-stabilizerness. Although the witness is not a ?nite-size resource monotone, it becomes sharply concentrated and e?ectively invariant under random Cli?ord transformations in the large-qubit limit, suggesting an asymptotically linear growth law for broad families of non-stabilizer states. Our results restore a meaningful geometric phase-space characterization of qubit stabilizer structure and provide an operational diagnostic of non-stabilizerness.

infographic.key_insight: State-adaptive optimization restores an exact discrete Wigner-phase-space picture for qubit stabilizer states and turns the optimized Wigner value into a practical witness of non-stabilizerness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides an operational, measurement-based diagnostic for identifying non-stabilizer resources in qubit systems, which is relevant for quantum hardware characterization and fault-tolerant resource tracking.
method: Optimize the discrete Wigner map over fixed phase-space partitions instead of using a single state-independent representation.
Select maximal probabilities across mutually unbiased bases to implement the optimization directly from measurement statistics.
Use the optimized Wigner value at the origin as a non-stabilizer witness, with stabilizer states saturating the pure-state lower bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract claims exact delta-function Wigner representations for all qubit stabilizer states, a universal lower bound saturated by stabilizers, and strong concentration under random Clifford transformations at large qubit number.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed witness is not a finite-size resource monotone, so interpretation for small systems or single-shot comparisons may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Optimized discrete Wigner representations and non-stabilizerness in qubit systems

title: A Cognitive-Aware QML-CRL Framework for Detecting Affinity and Romance-Investment Fraud
authors: Bibhas Adhikari, Ramya Srinivasan
abstract: We present a hybrid quantum-classical framework that detects affinity and romance-investment fraud by modelling the cognitive biases in a manipulative conversation. In our proposed framework, cognitive biases central to this fraud class are carried by dedicated qubits in a structured parameterized quantum circuit, together with a frame qubit makes the encoding sensitive to the temporal order of manipulative reframing, and a narrative qubit that aggregates co-occurrence through a trainable entanglement layer. The circuit parameters are trained jointly with a classical reinforcement-learning agent that decides, turn by turn, whether to flag the conversation, modeled as an optimal stopping problem. We evaluate the model's performance on synthetic conversations that include hard negatives, legitimate but urgent, and legitimate but pushy sales conversations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical detector for affinity and romance-investment fraud that encodes cognitive manipulation patterns in qubits and uses reinforcement learning to decide when to flag a conversation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It suggests a structured quantum representation for sequential fraud cues, combined with an optimal-stopping RL policy for turn-by-turn intervention in conversational security systems.
method: Dedicated qubits encode key cognitive biases involved in manipulation.
A frame qubit captures temporal order of reframing; a narrative qubit aggregates co-occurrence via trainable entanglement.
A classical RL agent jointly trains with the quantum circuit to decide whether to flag the conversation at each turn.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model is evaluated on synthetic conversations, including hard negatives and legitimate urgent or pushy sales scenarios.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on synthetic data, so real-world robustness and transfer to live conversational fraud remain unproven.
infographic.paper_title: A Cognitive-Aware QML-CRL Framework for Detecting Affinity and Romance-Investment Fraud

title: CV-QAOA: Efficient Low-Depth Quantum Optimization of Continuous Variables
authors: Sriram Bharadwaj, Di Luo, Leo Zhou
abstract: We study a Continuous-Variable Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CV-QAOA) for high-dimensional continuous optimization. Our formulation extends an earlier CV-QAOA proposal with a variationally optimized initial state and recovers the convergence guarantees of Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) in the high-depth limit. We prove rigorous performance guarantees of CV-QAOA on several families of cost functions. First, we show $d$-step CV-QAOA minimizes any $d$-dimensional strictly convex quadratic function with $2d$ quantum queries to the cost function. We then analyze a family of nonconvex "Rotated Double Well" (RDW) functions with $2^d$ local minima introduced by arXiv:2311.00811. While prior work showed QHD reaches its global minimum with $\tilde O(d^3)$ queries, we prove that 1-step CV-QAOA solves RDW with just two quantum queries. Although general-purpose classical solvers need superpolynomial time for RDW and structure-awareness can reduce the cost to polynomial time, we show that the 1-step CV-QAOA protocol can be efficiently dequantized, and that a gradient-aligned line search succeeds with $O(d)$ queries, nearly matching the information-theoretic $Ω(d/\log d)$ query lower bound. To move beyond the dequantizable regime, we introduce a ``Rotated Square Well'' (RSW) problem, whose globally flat landscape suppresses useful local gradient information. For this family, we show that an adiabatic evolution simulated by CV-QAOA can reach the global minimum using $d^{o(1)}$ queries. On the other hand, any classical algorithm that learn the hidden rotation in RSW provably requires $Ω(d^2/\log d)$ queries, a bound we nearly match with an explicit $Θ(d^2\log d)$-query classical algorithm.Numerical simulations on deflected corrugated spring and Easom functions illustrate the promising performance of CV-QAOA on more general problems.

infographic.key_insight: CV-QAOA extends continuous-variable quantum optimization with variational initialization and strong query-complexity guarantees, matching or nearly matching optimal performance on several structured continuous problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results suggest low-depth quantum circuits may offer practical advantages for high-dimensional continuous optimization, especially when problem structure can be exploited or classical dequantization is limited.
method: Uses a variationally optimized initial state within CV-QAOA.
Proves exact or near-optimal query bounds for convex quadratics, Rotated Double Well, and Rotated Square Well families.
Compares quantum performance against classical lower bounds, dequantized line search, and numerical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports rigorous query-complexity proofs plus numerical simulations on deflected corrugated spring and Easom test functions.
infographic.watch_item: Several gains are problem-class specific, and one key protocol is explicitly dequantizable, so practical quantum advantage may depend on avoiding cases with exploitable gradient structure.
infographic.paper_title: CV-QAOA: Efficient Low-Depth Quantum Optimization of Continuous Variables

title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
authors: George Kourousias, Sergio Carrato, Roberto Pugliese, Aljoša Hafner, Francesco Guzzi, Matteo Billè
abstract: Which execution details must a quantum computation retain, and to what precision, to support a declared comparison? We define a sufficient record by the largest Hellinger distance between outcome laws that share it. Our main result is a circuit-derived certificate for continuous recording precision: independent channel-mixture probabilities enter through the affinity of latent noise flags, while coherent rotation differences enter through conditional quantum fidelity. Their joint composition bounds whole record cells without simulating their outcome distributions. For four-qubit QAOA at depth one, a 13-bit comparison record guarantees distance below 0.05 throughout a declared continuous noise box, uniformly over programmed angles when comparisons hold the logical task fixed. A construction with observable noise flags attains the general bound. Exact tensorization of Hellinger affinity connects recording precision to the length of a future measurement transcript. On finite context classes, separation witnesses certify minimum-cost field retention; a four-field record is the unique minimum for 28 archived QAOA instances. Fresh six-qubit processor measurements establish different minimum label counts at one common tolerance: two labels are necessary and sufficient for raw laws, while one suffices after a fixed decoder for a synthetic image-segmentation task. These hardware conclusions are conditional on stationary independent shots and remain distinct from the analytic channel certificate. Shared task definitions and evidential archives are retained separately. The framework specifies which execution distinctions matter, how precisely to record them, and what evidence supports the resulting agreement guarantee.

infographic.key_insight: The paper defines a principled notion of "sufficient quantum provenance" by identifying which execution details and recording precision are enough to guarantee a bounded difference between quantum outcome distributions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum hardware and workflow engineers a certificate for deciding what provenance to keep, at what precision, to support reproducible comparisons without fully simulating outcomes.
method: Uses Hellinger distance as the sufficiency criterion for shared records.
Derives a circuit-level certificate combining channel-mixture noise flags and coherent rotation differences via affinity and fidelity.
Applies the framework to QAOA and hardware measurements to determine minimum record fields and label counts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 13-bit comparison record keeping Hellinger distance below 0.05 for four-qubit depth-1 QAOA across a noise box, plus archival and hardware evaluations showing a four-field minimum record and task-dependent label counts.
infographic.watch_item: The hardware conclusions rely on stationary independent shots, so the guarantees may not extend directly to drift, correlated noise, or changing experimental conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
